records.name: Berlin
records.summary:
Germany's Pride movement faces a documented rise in attacks: the amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-motivated attacks on Pride events nationally in 2024 and 30 in 2025 across roughly 120 parades, including a boiling-water attack, and runs a €100,000 support fund weighted to eastern Germany. Ahead of the 2025 Christopher Street Day, with hundreds of thousands expected, Berlin's organisers nonetheless urged participants to 'be vigilant'.

The reporting also situates the capital: Maneo, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, states that big-city parades like Berlin's had not been specifically threatened — smaller towns are hardest to police — while everyday hostility still surfaces: one Berlin-Neukölln queer café owner reports 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in eighteen months.

records.name: Hessen
records.summary:
A Hessen Landtag small inquiry with the Interior Minister's answer (April 2025) records police-registered queer-hostile offences rising from 33 in 2022 to 83 in 2023 and 135 in 2024 — a year-on-year jump of 52 that the minister's reply calls alarming.

The trend must be read with the federal BKA's own caveat: its situation report on LSBTIQ* security introduced a new reporting category that makes state-by-state comparison possible but warns that classification changes can inflate registered counts, so rises may partly reflect better recording rather than a sharper danger. The same answer notes the 2010-established network of LSBTIQ* liaison officers in every police headquarters, governed by a standing framework concept — an institutional response in place while the statistics remain ambiguous.

records.name: Sachsen-Anhalt
records.summary:
Sachsen-Anhalt is one of three Länder — with Sachsen and Thüringen — that brought a Bundesrat initiative (reported June 2026) to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act on legal gender change, proposing an 'abuse review' mechanism with objective, documentable grounds for registry-office intervention. The trigger cited is the 'Fall Liebich' — a convicted far-right extremist whose legal gender was changed after sentencing.

The initiative is an attempt, not a change: it is backed by Union MPs, resisted by the SPD, and runs against a scheduled federal evaluation of the SBGG that the family ministry is conducting and whose SPD-led ministries consider the existing law sufficient. No standing administrative ban or documented street-attack pattern specific to this state was identified in the research pass.
